title: Field scenarios & counter-scripts: LLM API competitive angles
content:
PURPOSE
Quick field reference for SDR/AEs/SEs: short scripts, competitive angles, and proof points to use when prospects compare Redwood Inference to other LLM API providers. Focused on situation-driven objections (latency, cost at scale, private deployments, reliability, and observability). Not a canonical battlecard — this is tactic-first, scenario-based.

PRINCIPLES / ONE-LINERS (pick one depending on buyer)
- Engineering-first inference platform: same API across hosted, dedicated, and private so integrations are low lift and rollouts predictable.
- Control for unit economics: we give you levers (batching, caching, quantization) that meaningfully reduce per-token spend without sacrificing quality.
- Production reliability: multi-tier routing, model fallbacks, and SLA-backed dedicated capacity keep apps online.

TOP SCENARIOS + SCRIPTS (short, usable in a call)
1) Latency-sensitive consumer feature (real-time chat / assistant)
  Assumption: prospect experienced jitter/large p95 from public LLM APIs.
  Common objection: "Third-party APIs are simpler — why switch?"
  Quick script: "Totally — public APIs are quick to start. What tends to break is consistency at scale. With Redwood you get the same simple API but the option to pin to Dedicated pools and automatic KV-prefix caching so your p95 stabilizes across load. We’ve seen customers cut p95 variance by ~2x during peak traffic with dedicated routing + caching. Want a short perf run against your sample prompt set?"
  Demo hook / data point: show route-level p95 dashboard and one-minute spike behavior.
  Follow-up asset: perf-run-1203 (internal trace).

2) Cost-conscious scale-up (embedding-heavy search; millions of tokens/day)
  Assumption: price per token is top-of-mind, prospect compares cost numbers.
  Objection: "We can get cheaper per-token elsewhere."
  Quick script: "Price alone hides unit economics — how many tokens do you re-send? With prefix caching and smarter batching we reduce tokens sent and average GPU time per token. For similar quality we commonly reduce effective spend 20–40% through runtime optimizations. If you give a day of traffic we’ll show a cost-savings projection with our recommended quantization + batching profile."
  Tactical play: propose a 7‑day pilot on a small Dedicated pool to produce actual billing simulation.

3) Enterprise / regulated workloads (banking, health)
  Assumption: data residency and auditability are blockers for public APIs.
  Objection: "How do we keep PII out of vendor logs?"
  Quick script: "We offer Private deployments (VPC & on-prem) with customer-managed KMS and audit logs. The control plane can be isolated and audit records retained to your retention policy. We will also sign bespoke DPA/SOC terms as part of an enterprise contract. Would a PoC on a VPC deployment help unblock security review?"
  Proof points: list of integrations (KMS, HSM) and enterprise customer reference (anonymized).

4) Model quality drift and evaluation risk
  Assumption: buyer fears regressions when providers push new models/weights.
  Objection: "If you change models or quantize, we risk regressions in output."
  Quick script: "Redwood separates model lifecycle from routing: you pin model versions, run canary rollouts, and tie changes to eval suites. Our Optimize suggestions are conservative and we surface regression alerts against your prompt set. We can run a model-change simulation against your most critical prompts before you accept the rollout."
  Tactical: offer an example regression report and explain rollback policy.

5) Migration friction vs "just keep using the vendor"
  Assumption: product teams hate migrations.
  Objection: "We don’t want the integration work and risk of replacing current APIs."
  Quick script: "We prioritize a drop-in experience: REST/SDK parity, and a migration checklist from our Solutions Engineering team. For critical endpoints we can set up split-routing (send 10% of traffic to Redwood) so you can validate behavior without full cutover. What endpoint would you want to test first?"
  Follow-up: propose a 2-week trial with split routing and dedicated SE time.

COMPETITIVE PATTERNS (how rivals usually position themselves and how to counter)
- Rival: 'cheapest per-token' providers
  Their play: headline per-token price, simple docs.
  Counter: highlight unit-economics, caching, and end-to-end costs (retries, network, latency SLO misses). Use example savings projection from a real pilot.

- Rival: 'model-first marketplaces'
  Their play: many models, easy swapping.
  Counter: emphasize production guarantees — model catalog is curated + performance profiles; switching is supported but we add routing safety nets and rollout tooling to avoid surprise customer-facing regressions.

- Rival: 'single-tenant hosts / managed endpoints'
  Their play: security and isolation.
  Counter: match with Redwood Private and Dedicated but push value-adds: live observability, fallback policies, and cost controls that many hosts don't provide out of the box.

PROOF POINTS & FAST FACTS (one-liners you can memorize)
- "Dedicated pools with SLA-backed latency targets — used by customers with 5M+ monthly requests."
- "Typical effective spend reduction 20–40% after applying batching + caching recommendations."
- "We support private VPC/on-prem installs with customer-managed KMS and audit logs for regulated customers."
- "Rollouts tied to eval suites and automatic regression alerts — rollback in minutes."

TRAPS (what to avoid saying / pitfalls)
- Don’t overpromise exact % cost savings without a pilot dataset.
- Don’t claim parity with every open model; be specific about models we’ve benchmarked.
- Avoid deep technical rebuttals if you’re not an SE — use the SE team for kernel-/quantization debates.

SE TACTICAL CHECKLIST (what to prep when prospect asks for a technical deep-dive)
- Collect: sample prompts, typical sequence length, peak qps, current p95 latency, daily token volume.
- Offer: small Dedicated pool perf run, split routing, or a VPC PoC depending on buyer stage.
- Deliverables: route-level latency dashboard, cost-savings projection, regression report for top 20 prompts.

EXAMPLE OBJECTION Q&A (short)
Q: "We’re worried you’ll change the model and outputs will be different."
A: "We don’t flip models on you — you pin versions and can run canaries. We’ll run your eval set and give you the pass/fail report before any rollout."

Q: "What about inference cost?"
A: "We look at effective cost. Typical levers we use: KV-prefix caching, batch sizing tuned to your latency profile, and quantization where quality permits. We’ll produce a projection from a short pilot so you can compare apples to apples."

Q: "How do you handle outages or region-level constraints?"
A: "Smart routing — automatic fallback to compatible model variants or other regions. Can also configure burst capacity on Dedicated to absorb regional spikes."

NEXT ACTION SCRIPTS (close motions)
- Low friction eval: "Can you share a sample of 24 hours of traffic and 10–20 canonical prompts? We’ll run a perf+cost simulation and return a short deck in 5 business days."
- Enterprise: "We’ll scope a VPC PoC: 2-week pilot, audit log verification, and an SE-led integration plan. If the security team signs off, we’ll map a migration plan during that pilot."

ATTACHMENTS / ASSETS TO SHARE AFTER CALL
- One-pager: 'Redwood performance and cost playbook' (internal pdf)
- Sample deck: 'Dedicated pool pilot: what we measure'
- Example regression report (anonymized)

NOTES TO REP / LANE HINTS
- For product-led buyers: emphasize low-friction API and transparent per-route metrics.
- For infra/ops buyers: lead with VPC, KMS, audit logs and rollout controls.
- For finance buyers: ask for daily token volume and send a modeled cost comparison rather than headline per-token numbers.

TODO / OPEN QUESTIONS
- Get updated internal SLO numbers for p95 on small prompts (ask SRE for current benchmark).
- Collect 2 anonymized case studies showing 'post-migration cost delta' with permission for redacted numbers.

END - keep this doc lean and add practitioner notes after real calls.
